beats.text: In 1838, a militia marched more than 800 Potawatomi out of Indiana at gunpoint. It started at Twin Lakes, near Plymouth.
beats.label: TWIN LAKES, NEAR PLYMOUTH, INDIANA
beats.credit: History: Citizen Potawatomi Nation; Indiana Public Media

beats.text: Their leader, Menominee, had refused to give up his people's land. So the governor sent General John Tipton and a volunteer militia.
beats.label: MARSHALL COUNTY, 1838
beats.credit: Citizen Potawatomi Nation; Indiana Public Media

beats.text: On September 4, the march began. Menominee and two other leaders were held under guard in a wagon. The militia burned the village so no one could return.
beats.label: SEPTEMBER 4, 1838
beats.credit: Indiana Public Media; Potawatomi Cultural Heritage Center

beats.text: They traveled about 660 miles, to what is now eastern Kansas. It took 2 months.
beats.label: INDIANA TO KANSAS
beats.credit: Indiana Public Media; Citizen Potawatomi Nation

beats.text: At least 42 people died on the way, many of them children. It became known as the Trail of Death.
beats.label: THE TRAIL OF DEATH
beats.credit: Potawatomi Cultural Heritage Center; Kansas Heritage

beats.text: Today, markers follow the route across 4 states. And near Twin Lakes, a statue of Menominee has stood since 1909.
beats.label: TODAY
beats.credit: Citizen Potawatomi Nation; National Register of Historic Places
